India VIX at 16.2 is moderate, so no hard override applies, and cheap valuations (P/E at the 4th percentile), PCR of 1.31 and DII absorption of +67k cr argue against maximum de-risking, so the multiplier sits at 0.65 rather than 0.5. Tilts follow the rotation map plus the macro drivers. IT is overweight as a leader with rising delivery and an INR tailwind, and Telecom is overweight as a defensive leader. Energy and Consumer Discr. are underweight because crude hurts OMCs, paints and aviation. Industrials and Materials are underweight as lagging cyclicals with very weak breadth. Financials stay neutral despite the RBI cut bias, given 16% breadth and falling delivery; note that the repo rate is inconsistent in the inputs (6.0% vs 5.5%).

fundamental.thesis: Adani Enterprises is the Adani group's incubator conglomerate (airports, roads, data centres, copper, new energy and mining services), so I judged it on EV/EBITDA and execution rather than P/E. Q2FY27, derived from the official H1 and Q1 filings, shows revenue of about ₹36,594 cr, up roughly 76% YoY and accelerating from +49.5% in Q1 after -10% in H1FY26; PAT was about ₹919 cr, a 2.5% margin. Most of that growth comes from a low-margin copper segment that rose 1,244% to ₹25,483 cr in H1, while roads fell 69%, finance costs rose 46%, and H1 PAT swung to a ₹241 cr loss partly due to a ₹2,644 cr OFAC settlement. On valuation, EV/EBITDA of 36.5x and P/B of 4.8x against an ROE of 13.7% look expensive for a leveraged, FCF-negative capex story (FCF of -₹10,800 cr in H1, -₹31,012 cr in FY26). Forward P/E of 53.6x is above trailing 41.1x, FY EPS estimates were cut 22% in the last 30 days, and the stock sits at 98.5% of its 52-week range. The peer block compares it with oil and gas names, which flatters the gap, but the expensive verdict holds on absolute multiples too. The biggest risk is that continued heavy debt-funded capex, with interest coverage at only 2.8x, keeps eroding earnings while the market prices in perfection.

fundamental.thesis: Power Grid Corporation is India's dominant inter-state transmission utility, earning a regulated ROE (~15.5%) on an expanding fixed-asset base — a classic annuity where earnings growth equals capex commissioned rather than tariff or volume swings. Revenue grew a modest +2.7% YoY to ₹11,497 cr in Q1FY27, but PAT declined -0.9% YoY to ₹3,598 cr with PAT margin compressing from 34.7% in FY25 to 31.3% in Q1FY27; the core transmission segment (80% of revenue) delivered only +2.2% growth, suggesting asset commissioning pace has slowed even as consultancy revenue surged +27.75% YoY. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive regulated business (per sector card), POWERGRID trades at 10.7× EV/EBITDA vs a peer median of 11.6× and sits at P25 on both trailing P/E (14.2×) and EV/EBITDA within its Utilities peer group — a consistent cheap signal, though 90-day EPS revisions of -3.0% signal the market is trimming growth expectations. The biggest risk is the upcoming CERC regulatory reset combined with near-term earnings compression: current ratio of 0.57 signals working capital strain, forward P/E exceeds trailing (indicating expected earnings softness), and the three JV/subsidiary divestments (including CTUIL reclassified as held-for-sale) introduce balance-sheet uncertainty until completion.

fundamental.thesis: Wipro is India's fourth-largest IT services exporter and lags tier-1 peers on growth; the sector is in an AI-driven reset where legacy time-and-materials revenue is shrinking. H1FY27 revenue rose 9.8% YoY to ₹49,231 cr, a sharp pickup from near-flat FY26 (Q4FY26 at -0.2%), but PAT slipped 0.7% to ₹6,556 cr and PAT margin has compressed from 14.7% to 13.3% over the trend window. The revenue pickup probably owes part of its size to the Mindsprint acquisition and a weak rupee rather than real organic demand, and several trend rows look inconsistent, so the figures are unreliable. Using trailing P/E and EV/EBITDA as the yardsticks, Wipro is cheap: 15.6x P/E against a 22–30x sector band and a 24.7x peer median, and 10.5x EV/EBITDA, the lowest among its 8 peers. Cash conversion is strong (CFO/PAT 1.31x, net cash about ₹5,900 cr). The stock sits near its 52-week low. Sell-side coverage is heavily bearish (19 of 40 rate it sell) and estimates are drifting down, so the low multiple may be a value trap rather than mispricing.

Adani Ports is India's largest private port operator, and its port and SEZ business plus a growing logistics and marine arm earn infrastructure-like EBITDA margins of around 60%. For H1 FY27, revenue rose 21.1% YoY to ₹22,161 cr and PAT rose 14.0% to ₹7,332 cr. Working back from the filings, Q2 FY27 alone was about ₹11,340 cr revenue (around +24% YoY) and ₹3,682 cr PAT (around +18% YoY), a re-acceleration from Q1's +18.6% revenue and +10.2% PAT, though still below the +30% revenue growth of H1 FY26. EBITDA margin is stable at about 60%, and operating cash flow is 1.82x PAT, so profits are backed by cash. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for capital-intensive businesses, the stock trades at 21.0x against a peer median of 34.0x (P24), with trailing P/E of 31.2x and forward P/E of 23.5x. That looks cheap on paper, but the comparison set is high-multiple capital-goods and defence names (ABB, CGPOWER, HAL) rather than port operators. Against the 28–45x industrials P/E band, with the stock at 96% of its 52-week range, I grade it fair rather than cheap. The main risks are acquisition-led leverage, with net debt at ₹49,686 cr (1.86x EBITDA) and capex at about 24% of revenue, plus logistics margins that fell to 8.6% from 14.0% YoY, in a risk-off, crude-heavy macro backdrop.

fundamental.thesis: Coal India is the dominant domestic coal miner, and its returns come mainly from sales volume plus the premium it earns on e-auction coal. Government-set prices and a high dividend payout drive most of the shareholder return. For H1 FY27, revenue rose 13.8% YoY to ₹90,434 cr and PAT rose 18.9% to ₹15,397 cr, with a 17.0% PAT margin and a 28.5% EBITDA margin. Cash backing is strong: operating cash flow was 2.21x PAT. However, the trend table mixes half-year, nine-month and full-year periods, so the 'decelerating' and 'contracting' signals are not like-for-like. Earnings also include a ₹841 cr stripping-provision reversal, so underlying growth is somewhat lower than the headline. On the sector card's yardstick (P/E 6–10x plus dividend yield for PSUs), a trailing P/E of 9.2x (forward 8.1x) and EV/EBITDA of 6.1x sit at the peer median (P50), so the stock is fair, or 'policy-priced', rather than cheap. That is especially true with the price at 85% of its 52-week range. The main risk is cost creep from the NCWA-XIII wage provision (₹499 cr) and cess disputes, which could erode margins if government-administered prices are not raised to match.

fundamental.thesis: Nestle India is a leading packaged-food company (MAGGI, NESCAFE, KITKAT, infant nutrition) with deep rural and urban distribution and a premium brand franchise. In Q2FY27, revenue rose 20.5% YoY to ₹6,782 cr and PAT rose 36.3% to ₹1,027 cr (15.1% PAT margin), with double-digit volume growth reported across all product groups. Growth is slowing slightly from Q1FY27, when revenue grew 25.4% and PAT 47.9%. EBITDA margin dipped slightly to 23.8% from 24.2%, and ad spend rose 46%, so margins are not being protected by cutting brand investment. On the P/E yardstick for FMCG staples, trailing P/E of 77x sits above the sector norm of 40-65x and above the peer median of 51.5x (P83), and forward P/E of 59x is the most expensive in the sector (P100), so the stock is expensive. The biggest risk is a valuation de-rating: the current 11% volume growth is far above the company's 5-year volume CAGR of 4.2%, and the price assumes it lasts while cocoa and milk costs keep pressing on margins.

Asian Paints is India's largest decorative paints company, a consumer franchise inside the Materials label, and it now faces a structurally tougher market since Birla Opus entered. Revenue growth has accelerated from +2.8% (H1FY26) to +17.5% (H1FY27, ₹20,518 cr), and the implied Q2FY27 quarter was about ₹9,976 cr (+17% YoY). That growth is mostly price-led: decorative volume rose +6.4% against value growth of +14.5%. Profitability is weakening inside it: implied Q2 PAT of about ₹1,086 cr gives a 10.9% margin, down from 14.8% in Q1; Q2 consolidated PBDIT margin fell 202 bps to 15.6% on raw-material inflation; and H1 cash conversion dropped to 0.72x CFO/PAT from 1.64x in FY26. I graded valuation on the paints-franchise P/E yardstick from the sector card (30–60x), not the cyclical Materials peer median. On that basis a trailing P/E of 58.9x sits at the top of the band, with only forward P/E of 45.4x offering relief, so I call it expensive for a business whose margins are compressing. Separately, the snapshot's 102% dividend yield and 17.85 debt/equity look like data errors and were ignored. The biggest risk is that crude-linked input inflation, made worse by a weak rupee, keeps outrunning the staggered price increases while competition limits how much more can be passed on.

fundamental.thesis: JSW Steel is one of India's largest integrated steelmakers, running at 88% utilisation, with record Q2FY27 crude steel output of 7.27 MT and sales of 7.46 MT (+13% YoY), helped by auto demand (+36%) and a protected domestic steel market. Revenue growth accelerated from +9.8% YoY in Q1FY27 to +20.6% in Q2FY27 (₹54,486 cr), and PAT rose to ₹5,359 cr at a 9.8% margin; the reported +225.6% PAT growth and the 'contracting margin' signal are both distorted, because FY26's 13.8% margin includes an ₹18,051 cr one-off gain from deconsolidating BPSL and comparatives are restated, so on an underlying basis margins are roughly stable to improving, while EBITDA per tonne is +24% YoY but down QoQ from ₹14,990 to ₹13,329. Using EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick for steel, the 12.6× trailing multiple sits above the 5–8× mid-cycle steel norm, even though peers rank it P20, a ranking flattered by paints and adhesives names in the comparison set; the 13.8× trailing P/E is also flattered by the one-off gain, and forward P/E of 17.3× is higher. With the stock at 92% of its 52-week range, valuation reads as fair at best, not cheap. The main risk is spread compression during a heavy ₹22–24k cr capex year: coking coal and power costs are rising with crude and a weak rupee, while EBITDA per tonne has already started to slip QoQ.

fundamental.thesis: Tata Steel is India's largest integrated steel producer (~35 MTPA capacity) with significant global operations in the UK (TSUK) and Netherlands (TSN), making it a spread-cycle business where EBITDA margin per tonne is the primary value driver — not PAT, which is distorted by depreciation and interest. FY26 revenue grew +6.2% YoY to ₹2,32,140 cr with PAT recovering +243% to ₹10,886 cr on a low base; Q1FY27 EBITDA margin expanded 134 bps YoY to 15.4% (the key sector KPI, and a positive signal), though PAT margin has dipped to 3.9% vs FY26's 4.7% run-rate — partly reflecting an extraordinary ₹294 cr depreciation charge with a further ₹1,178 cr expected in FY27; CFO/PAT of 2.52× confirms cash-backed earnings quality. fundamental.thesis: Eternal (formerly Zomato) runs India's leading food-delivery platform plus Blinkit, the quick-commerce business, which is now 78.5% of revenue. Official H1FY27 filings show revenue up 113.7% YoY to ₹44,349 cr and PAT up 141.1% to ₹217 cr, but growth has slowed from +168.5% in FY26 and PAT margin has narrowed from 0.7% to 0.5%. Most of that revenue comes from Blinkit (₹34,816 cr, +183%) at only a 2.5% segment margin, while food delivery (+36.9%, 19.5% margin) still earns most of the profit, and Hyperpure (-34%) and Going Out (-18.7% margin) are a drag. Free cash flow was also negative at ₹-1,378 cr for H1. On valuation, P/E is not a useful yardstick for a platform like this, so I used EV/sales, growth delivery and unit economics. On those terms, 4.2× sales on revenue earning roughly 4–5% EBITDA, an EV/EBITDA of about 193× and a forward P/E of 61× (the most expensive of 20 sector peers, P100) grade it as expensive. The biggest risk is that the business has not yet shown it can reach Blinkit's long-term 4–6% margin target while competition stays intense: analysts have cut current-year EPS estimates by 35% in 30 days even though 29 of 32 still rate it a buy, which is a classic pattern before a stock de-rates.

Trent runs Westside, Zudio and the Star grocery format, with 1,342 fashion stores in 339 cities, and is one of India's leading premium-to-value apparel retailers. Q2 FY27 is derived from the H1FY27 and Q1FY27 rows, so it carries some uncertainty because those rows don't fully reconcile. On that basis, revenue was about ₹5,873 cr, up about 15% YoY from ₹5,107 cr, and PAT was about ₹468 cr, up about 25% from ₹373 cr. That suggests growth slowed from the 18–20% reported for Q1 and H1, even though the pre-computed signal says 'accelerating'. Margins are genuinely improving: H1 EBITDA margin rose to 14.1% from 12.5%, Q2 operating EBIT margin rose to 11.6% from 10.5%, and PAT growth is understated because the year-ago quarter included a ₹96 cr one-time asset sale gain. Same-store sales growth was only 'low single digits' in Q4 FY26, so growth is mostly coming from new stores, and store additions are slowing (about 29 Westside and Zudio openings in Q2, and 25 in Q1). Using EV/EBITDA plus unit economics as the yardstick for a store-led retailer, valuation is expensive: EV/EBITDA is 55.3x, the highest in the sector (median 21.9x), and trailing P/E is 85.4x versus a 39.7x peer median. That P/E does sit inside the dossier's 60–100x band for premium franchises, and the stock is already at 1.7% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that a rich multiple meets slowing store-driven growth, weak like-for-like sales, a risk-off macro backdrop with rising crude, and slightly negative EPS revisions, which is the setup in which these names de-rate sharply on any guidance reset.

H1FY27 revenue grew +16.4% YoY to ₹38,439 cr (steady within a consistent +13–16% band over six periods), but PAT grew only +10.0% to ₹1,603 cr as PAT margin contracted to 4.17% from 4.4% — finance costs surged 84% to fund aggressive expansion, the Avenue E-commerce subsidiary dragged ₹166.62 cr in losses, and CFO/PAT collapsed from 0.96× (H1FY26) to 0.34× (H1FY27), signalling a meaningful deterioration in earnings quality. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary valuation yardstick (capital-intensive retail with PAT margins distorted by lease and e-commerce costs), DMART trades at 52.4× EV/EBITDA — P100 (most expensive) among 13 Consumer Discr. peers and +51% above the sector median — while trailing P/E of 89.1× is also P100 and +73% above sector median; sell-side EPS estimates have been revised down -3.1% over 90 days, a textbook pre-derating signal. The biggest risk is that the quick-commerce threat from Blinkit erodes SSSG momentum just as e-commerce losses widen and leverage builds, triggering the 25–40% multiple reset the sector card explicitly flags for any guidance disappointment at these premium valuations.

Pidilite is India's dominant adhesives and sealants franchise (Fevicol, M-Seal, Dr. Fixit), a consumer brand business rather than a commodity chemicals cyclical. H1FY27 revenue rose 21.1% YoY to Rs 8,849 cr and PAT rose 19.6% to Rs 1,510 cr, but the second quarter weakened. Backing Q2 out of the H1 and Q1 filings gives revenue of about Rs 4,297 cr (+21% YoY) but PAT of only about Rs 626 cr (+8% YoY), against Q1 PAT growth of +29.8%. Implied EBITDA margin fell from 28.6% in Q1 to about 22% in Q2, and H1 cash conversion slipped to 0.73x CFO/PAT from 1.15x in FY26. On the consumer-franchise yardstick the sector card prescribes (30–60x P/E, not steel or chemicals multiples), a trailing P/E of 57.1x and forward 46.8x sit at the top of the band, so the grade is fair-to-stretched. The P100 peer rank is distorted by steel and metal names, and Pidilite still trades below the paint peers BERGEPAINT and ASIANPAINT. The main risk is that sales growth stays strong while margins keep shrinking from crude-linked input costs and a weak rupee, which would make the premium multiple hard to sustain.

Valuation looks fair: I graded it on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-heavy cement business, and at 18.5x it sits at the peer median (P53). The biggest risk is that margins keep shrinking from input-cost inflation, integrating several acquisitions and a soft European auto cycle, while the Q2FY27 results (trading window closed since 29 Sep) are imminent.

fundamental.thesis: LIC is India's dominant PSU life insurer (roughly 60% market share by first-year premium) with an unrivalled agency distribution franchise of ~1.3 million agents and an implicit government guarantee on policyholder liabilities — a structural moat no private peer can replicate at comparable scale. The latest clean data (H1FY26) shows PAT growth accelerating to +15.3% YoY (₹21,056 cr) while revenue grew a more modest +4.8% YoY (₹215,780 cr), implying margin expansion; the prior solo quarter (Q1FY26) showed PAT growth of only +5.0%, so the direction of PAT improvement is positive — but only two periods have complete data, preventing a robust multi-quarter trajectory call, and CFO/PAT of 0.70× in H1FY26 is below the 0.60 concern threshold only narrowly, suggesting earnings quality is acceptable but not pristine. The correct valuation yardstick for a life insurer is P/EV (Price-to-Embedded Value), which is unavailable here; using the next-best available proxy — P/B of 2.05× against a TTM ROE of 42.4% — LIC is unambiguously cheap on any reasonable framework, and the peer comparison reinforces this: LICI sits at P0 (absolute cheapest in its peer group) on trailing P/E, forward P/E, P/B, and EV/EBITDA simultaneously, trading at an -83.8% discount to the sector median P/E — a discount partly structural (PSU status, legacy product mix, government-directed social mandates) but appearing excessive in magnitude against a business generating 42% ROE. The single biggest near-term risk is management continuity: MD Dinesh Pant's government-approved voluntary retirement was announced on 25 Sep 2026, and in a PSU insurer context, leadership transitions can disrupt ongoing product mix improvement, agency productivity initiatives, and investor-relations momentum heading into Q2FY27 results.

InterGlobe Aviation (IndiGo) is India's dominant domestic airline with a 442-aircraft fleet, so the Industrials sector card's order-book lens does not apply and I judged it on airline unit economics (RASK vs CASK, load factor, fuel). In Q2FY27 revenue grew 25.9% YoY to ₹23,364 cr, accelerating from about +5% in FY26 and +19.9% in Q1FY27, but this came entirely from fares (yield +34.3%) while passengers fell 4.7%, capacity fell 1% and load factor slipped 2.2 pts to 80.3%. Profit went the other way: the company lost ₹1,879 cr, a -8.0% PAT margin, and EBITDA margin fell from about 24-25% a year ago to 10.5%, as fuel cost rose 67% and a ₹1,155 cr forex loss hit the quarter. On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive business, the stock trades at 16.4x, with a 21x forward P/E. That looks cheap against the Industrials peer median of about 34x, but those peers are capital-goods companies; for a loss-making airline with lease-heavy debt the multiple is roughly fair, not a bargain. Trailing P/E is not meaningful because of the losses, P/B of 27x is distorted by thin lease-adjusted equity, and the 24% dividend yield in the snapshot is almost certainly a data error. The biggest risk is the macro mix of crude above $102, the rupee at 95/USD and softening passenger volumes, which leaves the company dependent on fares holding up; FY EPS estimates have already been cut about 36% over 90 days.

fundamental.thesis: Zydus Lifesciences is a large Indian pharma company that earns from US generics, India branded formulations and consumer products, and it is now adding medtech and US specialty businesses through acquisitions (Amplitude Surgical, Comfort Click, Assertio). PAT fell -35.9% to ₹940 cr, EBITDA fell -9.3%, PAT margin compressed from about 18.6% (FY26) to 11.7%, and EBITDA margin dropped from 31.2% to 25.4%. Exceptional charges were only ₹18 cr, so the profit drop comes from the business itself and not from one-off items. US revenue was already shrinking (-5.7% in Q4 FY26), which means the earlier gRevlimid-type windfall is fading. On the desk's yardstick for pharma (P/E plus EV/EBITDA), the stock looks cheap on trailing numbers: P/E of 21.7x is below the 28-40x sector range and in the cheapest 8% of peers, and EV/EBITDA of 16.1x is about 25% below the peer median. However, forward P/E of 23.3x sits only 9% below the peer median, at P38, and is higher than trailing P/E, so earnings are expected to fall. With the stock at 90% of its 52-week range, I grade valuation as fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that Q2 results on 4 Nov confirm continued margin erosion from loss-making medtech (-28.9% segment margin) and falling US sales, at a time when the US Commerce review of tariffs on generics still hangs over the stock.

Torrent Pharma is a leading India branded-formulations company, mainly in chronic therapies, with export arms in Brazil, the US and Germany; the JB Pharma merger took effect in July 2026 and adds to the India franchise, which carries no US tariff risk. In Q2FY27 revenue rose 50.8% YoY to ₹4,979 cr, but most of that came from the acquisition: the base business grew about 18%, and base India grew 20% against a 12% market. PAT fell 9.6% YoY to ₹534 cr, and the PAT margin dropped from 17.9% to 10.7% even though EBITDA rose 54% and the EBITDA margin held at 33.5%, which suggests that costs below EBITDA from the deal are using up the operating gains. On valuation the stock is expensive whether you use P/E or EV/EBITDA (EV/EBITDA is the better measure while acquisition costs distort profit): trailing P/E is 69.1x against a pharma range of 28–40x and a peer median of 36.4x (P92), forward P/E is 46.5x, and EV/EBITDA is 37.5x against a peer median of 21.4x (P85). The biggest risk is that the market prices in a smooth integration while analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 5% over 30 days and 7% over 90 days and the stock sits at 81% of its 52-week range, so a slow merger payoff or German and JB-international weakness could pull the multiple down.

The implied Q2 revenue (about ₹4,258 cr) was below Q1's ₹4,431 cr, and PAT is growing more slowly than revenue because interest and depreciation from the capex build eat into the gains. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-heavy IPP. At 31.8× against a utilities peer median of 11.6× (P100 in sector), and P/B of 12.7× on an ROE of only 7.6%, the stock is clearly expensive. It also trades at 94% of its 52-week range while sell-side FY EPS estimates have been cut 14.5% over 90 days. fundamental.thesis: GAIL (India) is the country's dominant natural gas transmission and marketing company (~16,000 km pipeline network), with additional businesses in LPG, city gas distribution, and petrochemicals — a volume/tariff infrastructure story largely insulated from crude price swings per the sector card. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive infrastructure business (as the sector card prescribes), GAIL trades at 11.56× (P50 among energy peers) on a trailing basis, but its forward P/E of 9.46× is 34% below the sector median and ranks at P0 (cheapest in sector) on both forward P/E and P/B (1.26× vs peer median 2.6×), with 31 sell-side analysts lifting FY EPS estimates +12.7% over 90 days — grading cheap on a forward-earnings basis. fundamental.thesis: IOC is India's largest PSU oil marketing company and refiner, whose earnings are driven by the government's retail pricing policy as much as by crude — per the Sector Card, OMC margins rise when crude falls and collapse when it rises above frozen pump prices. Q1FY27 (Apr-Jun 2026) illustrates this fully: revenue surged 27.1% YoY to ₹2,81,933 cr on volume recovery, but consolidated PAT collapsed -123.9% YoY to a ₹1,141 cr net loss (vs ₹6,808 cr profit in Q1FY26), with the petroleum products segment swinging from +₹9,070 cr to -₹1,705 cr as elevated crude erased all marketing margins and EBITDA margin contracted from 7.9% → 6.6% → 4.2% → 1.9% across four periods — revenue growth is a volume/price passthrough artefact, not a sign of business strength. Trailing EV/EBITDA of 4.11× is 32% below the sector median of 6.1× and trailing P/E of 4.44× is well below the Sector Card's 6–10× PSU OMC benchmark, with IOC at P0 (cheapest) in its peer group on both P/E and P/B — screens cheap — but forward P/E of 7.7× above trailing signals expected further earnings deterioration, and as the Sector Card explicitly warns, this discount is 'policy-priced not mis-priced', a durable structural discount rather than a mean-reversion opportunity. The dominant risk is a material governance breach: the Audit Committee has been non-functional since March 2026 due to the absence of independent directors, a SEBI compliance lapse that undermines confidence in reported financials precisely when crude is at $89.72/bbl and rising, the cumulative LPG under-recovery buffer stands at -₹29,730 cr, and compensation is being drip-fed in monthly instalments.

United Spirits is India's largest spirits maker (Diageo-controlled), with a premium-heavy portfolio that gives it pricing power in a slow-growing staples sector. In the latest extracted quarter (Q1 FY27), revenue was ₹6,122 cr, up 5.1% YoY, and PAT was ₹463 cr, up 11.0% YoY. Revenue growth has edged up from +3.8% (9M FY26) to +3.9% (FY26) to +5.1%, and PAT margin has widened from 6.1% to 6.6% to 7.6%. Profit is growing faster than sales, which points to mix and cost gains rather than strong volume. No volume data is available to confirm real demand, and the Q2 FY27 results filed on 2026-10-28 have not been extracted yet, so the most recent quarter is still unverified. The yfinance Q2 rows (revenue ₹1,696 cr, PAT ₹460 cr) do not match the PDF-based scale and are disregarded. On valuation I used trailing P/E plus peer rank, which is the standard yardstick for FMCG. Trailing P/E is 51.5x, inside the 40–65x sector norm and exactly at the peer median (P50); EV/EBITDA is 37.5x, slightly pricier than peers (P67). That makes it fair, not cheap, even though the stock sits near its 52-week low (9% of range). Two snapshot fields look like data errors and were ignored: the 136% dividend yield, and the 4.61 debt/equity, which is likely a percentage figure since the company has historically carried little net debt. The 0.79x cash conversion on FY26 profit, small downward EPS revisions despite 19 of 25 analysts rating it a buy, and a fresh change-in-management disclosure all argue for caution.

fundamental.thesis: Canara Bank is a large public sector bank (62.93% GoI ownership) and one of India's top-5 lenders by advances (₹13.6L cr), with a franchise spanning retail, wholesale, and treasury segments; the key yardstick here is P/B vs ROE, per the sector card, not P/E. H1FY27 shows a notable bifurcation: PAT grew strongly +31.3% YoY to ₹10,562 cr on dramatically improved asset quality (Gross NPA 1.33%, Net NPA 0.30%, PCR 95.34%), but total income contracted -3.38% YoY — revenue trajectory has decelerated from +7.7% (FY26) to -3.4% (H1FY27), driven by treasury revenue declining -18% YoY and NIM compression (2.06% FY26 vs 2.51% in Q4FY26), while PAT margin has expanded from 11.7% (FY26) to 13.1% (H1FY27) on sharply lower credit costs. At P/B of 1.02× against ROE of 15.9%, the stock is unambiguously cheap by the sector card's prescribed lender yardstick — sector card benchmark is P/B < 1.5 with ROE > 12% = cheap — and sits at P0 (cheapest) in its 14-peer regional bank cohort on both trailing P/E (6.1×, -64% vs median 16.8×) and forward P/E (5.7×), though much of this structural discount is explained by PSU overhang and below-median CASA (29.86% vs private sector ~40%+). The single biggest risk is NIM pressure persisting through the deposit repricing cycle — NIM at 2.06% for FY26 is already thin for a PSU bank and any further compression from EBLR-linked loan repricing faster than deposit cost decline would erode the PAT margin expansion thesis and keep revenue growth negative.

Punjab National Bank is India's second-largest public-sector lender, with ₹13.4 lakh crore of advances that grew 14.7% YoY, led by MSME (+19.8%) and overseas loans (+62.7%). In Q2 FY27, total income rose 5.4% YoY to ₹38,185 cr and net profit rose 12.8% to ₹5,532 cr; asset quality keeps improving, with Gross NPA down from 3.19% to 2.95% to 2.55%, Net NPA at 0.25%, slippage at 0.77% and provision coverage at 97%, though the revenue trend is noisy because one period row looks inconsistent. Using the lender yardstick of price-to-book against ROE, the stock trades at 0.83x book against a 13% TTM ROE (17.3% in the latest quarter), which is about 44% below the regional-bank median P/B of 1.5x and in the bottom 15% of peers, so it grades as cheap; the trailing P/E of 6.75x is consistent with that but is not the main yardstick. The main concern is funding: cost of deposits rose from 2.50% to 2.74% YoY, CASA slipped from 37.0% to 36.6%, domestic deposits grew only 9.5% against 12.5% domestic loan growth, and treasury income fell 57%, all of which could cap the 2.6–2.7% margin guidance.

fundamental.thesis: Jindal Steel & Power is a large integrated domestic steelmaker in the middle of a big capacity ramp (15.6 MT, up from 12.6 MT a year ago), with 92% of sales in India and a rising share of flat products (61%). Q2FY27 revenue was ₹16,679 cr, up 42.7% YoY, the fourth straight quarter of faster growth (from +3.7% to +10.7% to +23.0% to +42.7%), driven by 27% higher sales volume (2.38 MT); EBITDA rose 34% to ₹2,504 cr (about ₹10,500 per tonne), but PAT grew only 21.4% to ₹771 cr (4.6% margin) because finance costs jumped 53% and EBITDA margin slipped from 16.0% to 15.0% YoY. On the sector card's yardstick for steel (EV/EBITDA, 5–8x at mid-cycle), 14.2x is expensive; it only looks fair against the 16-peer median (P33) because that median includes paint and adhesive companies, and the cheap forward P/E of 12.2x relies on earnings roughly tripling just as FY estimates have been cut 13.3% over 90 days. fundamental.thesis: Polycab is India's largest wires and cables maker, with about 30-31% of the organised market, and it has a fast-growing consumer electricals (FMEG) arm. In Q2FY27, revenue rose 53% YoY to ₹9,900 cr and PAT rose 43% to ₹990 cr, faster than Q1FY27 (+39% revenue, +32.8% PAT). PAT margin edged up to 10.0% from 9.4% in FY26, FMEG reached its first double-digit EBIT margin (10.1%), and cash conversion was strong (CFO/PAT 1.12x, net cash ₹4,520 cr). However, much of the headline growth comes from copper prices (copper up 40-45% in H1, passed on to customers): wire volumes grew only 10.5% and cable volumes only 5% YoY, while wires and cables revenue grew 47%. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA, which suits a capital-intensive industrial, plus peer rank. EV/EBITDA is 35.0x against a sector median of 34.0x (P53), and trailing P/E is 53.8x (P50 vs peers, above the static 28-45x Industrials band). Forward P/E is lower at 38.5x and analysts have raised estimates (+7.6% in 30 days), so the stock grades fair, not cheap, and it is at 99.8% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that copper-inflated revenue growth fades as metal prices settle, while UltraTech's entry into wires pressures share and margins at a valuation that leaves little room for disappointment.

AU Small Finance Bank is a mid-sized lender, mostly secured (vehicle loans, mortgages, gold loans, small-business credit), with best-in-class asset quality among small finance banks. It is awaiting final RBI approval to convert to a universal bank. H1FY27 PAT rose 44.9% YoY to Rs 1,654 cr on income up 18.9% to Rs 12,374 cr. The implied Q2 PAT of about Rs 858 cr is roughly +53% YoY, up from +37% in Q1, so earnings momentum is accelerating. That is supported by Q1 NIM of 5.9% (vs 5.65% for FY26), cost of funds easing 32bps, PCR at 85% and GNPA steady at 1.99%. Net NPA ticked up from 0.74% to 0.81%, and CASA is weak at 29%. Valuation uses the P/B + ROE yardstick for lenders: P/B of 3.64x against FY26 ROE of 14.2% is expensive, ranking at the 100th percentile of 15 regional-bank peers (median 1.5x) on both P/B and forward P/E (16.0x vs an 11.0x median). Strong forward earnings growth is already priced in. The biggest risk is that this premium multiple depends on the universal-bank conversion and continued margin expansion, and either one slipping in a risk-off tape could trigger a sharp derating.

fundamental.thesis: Federal Bank is a mid-sized Kerala-based private bank with a strong NRI deposit franchise (NRE/NRO deposits of about ₹1.19 lakh cr) and a ₹3.02 lakh cr loan book. In Q2FY27 net total income (NII ₹3,153 cr plus other income ₹1,490 cr, about ₹4,644 cr) grew +29.8% YoY and PAT hit a record ₹1,386 cr, up +45.1%, with loans growing +21.7% and NII +26.4%. Asset quality also improved: gross NPA fell steadily from 1.83% to 1.32% and net NPA from 0.48% to 0.17% over four quarters. The pre-computed trajectory signals are unreliable because the historical revenue rows mix different bases, so I relied on the filing KPIs instead. On the lender yardstick (P/B plus ROE), 1.95x book against an 11.7% TTM ROE (13.6% latest quarter) is fair in absolute terms, but it is pricier than regional-bank peers (P71 on P/B, P79 on forward P/E 13.3x) and the stock sits at 97% of its 52-week range, so the good news looks largely priced in. The main risks are margins and funding: NIM slipped from 3.74% in Q4FY26 to 3.32%, deposits grew slower than loans (+18.6% vs +21.7%), and the CASA ratio of 32% sits below the sector's 35–38% norm.

fundamental.thesis: Indian Bank is a mid-sized public-sector bank with a ₹8.74L cr deposit base and ₹7.11L cr of advances, and about two-thirds of its loans go to retail, agriculture and MSME borrowers (RAM 65%). In H1FY27 total income grew 16.1% YoY to ₹44,333 cr and PAT grew 28.1% to ₹6,897 cr, but Q2 includes a one-off NSE listing gain of ₹1,387 cr. Stripping it out, underlying PAT growth looks closer to high single digits, and the core trend is mixed. Gross NPA improved from 2.23% to 1.86% to 1.61% with PCR at 98%. Against that, NIM slipped from 3.37% to 3.24%, credit cost rose from 0.21% to 0.47% to 0.71% over three quarters, and deposits are growing slower than loans (12.5% vs 17.5% YoY). Using P/B against ROE (the lender yardstick), 1.44x book for a 15.4% ROE is cheap in absolute terms, but peers are similar: P/B is only at P43 and P/E (9.9x) at P29 among regional banks, so the grade is fair. Analysts raised FY EPS estimates by about 5% over 90 days, which supports the case. The main risk is that loans keep growing faster than deposits, pushing up funding costs and squeezing NIMs further just as credit costs rise.

Bank of India is a government-controlled public sector bank (73.4% government ownership) with a ₹9.27 lakh crore deposit base, growing advances about 16% YoY in FY26 against roughly 13.6% deposit growth. The extracted data is incomplete. FY26 PAT grew about 14-15% to roughly ₹10,500 cr, but core net interest income rose only 3% and NIM is a thin 2.52%. Gross NPA improved from 2.26% (Q3FY26) to 1.98% (FY26), and provision coverage rose to 94.45% in H1FY27. Profit growth is therefore coming from lower credit costs and other income, not from lending spreads, and the Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-10-23 have not been extracted yet, so the latest-quarter trend is unconfirmed. On the lender yardstick (price-to-book plus ROE), the stock trades at 0.74x book against a 12-15% ROE, the cheapest in its 15-bank peer set on P/B (P0) and about 50% below the 1.5x median, which grades as cheap. The main risk is margin squeeze: loans are growing faster than deposits, NII growth is flat, and the rate-cut cycle is repricing loan yields down faster than deposit costs, which could stall earnings once the boost from lower provisioning fades.

fundamental.thesis: Yes Bank is a mid-sized private bank (₹4.69 lakh cr assets, ₹2.73 lakh cr advances) still rebuilding after its 2020 rescue, with improving asset quality (GNPA 1.5% to 1.3%, NNPA 0.3% to 0.2%, PCR 81.9%) but only a 35.1% CASA ratio and a high 63% cost-to-income ratio. FY26 revenue grew just +1.5% to ₹36,928 cr, while PAT jumped +43.6% to about ₹3,512 cr off a low base, and Q4 NII grew +15.9% with advances up 11.1% and NIM rising to about 2.6-2.7%. Using the bank yardstick of price-to-book versus return on equity, a P/B of 1.47x is at the peer median (P50) but rich for a 7.1% ROE, which is well below the cost of equity and implies a fair P/B nearer 0.6-0.9x even on a recovery case, so I grade it expensive; trailing P/E of 20.6x also sits at P79 vs peers (median 16.8x). fundamental.thesis: LIC Housing Finance is India's second-largest housing finance company (HFC), backed by LIC of India, with ₹3.27 lakh crore in loan assets and 84.5% of the portfolio in individual home loans — a conservative, low-risk mix. Q1FY27 showed a diverging picture: revenue declined 1.4% YoY to ₹7,083 crore (decelerating from +1.8% in Q3FY26 and reversing into negative territory), while PAT grew 9.9% YoY to ₹1,499 crore on margin expansion to 21.2%; however, NIM compressed sequentially from 2.8% (Q4FY26) to 2.6% (Q1FY27) and loan growth decelerated to 3.36% YoY from 4.39% in FY26 — both leading indicators pointing to slower earnings momentum ahead. Valuation yardstick is P/B + ROE (per the sector card for lenders): at P/B 0.75× against ROE of 14%, LICHSGFIN is unambiguously cheap by the 'P/B < 1.5, ROE > 12% = cheap' benchmark and ranks P0 (cheapest) among 34 Financials peers on trailing P/E (5.29× vs sector median 17.5×), a discount that partly reflects justified concerns but also likely overshoots fair value. The single largest risk is the combination of ongoing NIM compression and an active management transition (new MD/CEO appointment via postal ballot), which together create near-term uncertainty over both the liability-side repricing trajectory and strategic continuity in a rising-cost-of-funds environment.

fundamental.thesis: M&M Financial Services is Mahindra group's rural and semi-urban vehicle-finance NBFC, lending mainly for tractors, utility vehicles and used vehicles, and growing into SME loans (+32%) and loans against property (+41%). H1 FY27 revenue rose 16.3% YoY to ₹11,654 cr and PAT rose 67.9% to ₹1,838 cr. From the H1 and Q1 figures, Q2 revenue was about ₹5,936 cr (+18% YoY) and PAT about ₹911 cr (+61% YoY). Part of that PAT jump comes from a weak, high-provision H1 FY26 base. PAT was roughly flat quarter on quarter (₹927 cr to ₹911 cr), and FY26 AUM growth (12%) and disbursement growth (6%) were modest. As an NBFC this is judged on price-to-book versus ROE, not P/E. At 1.52× book with a TTM ROE of 11.9%, it sits just outside the 'cheap' rule (below 1.5× book with ROE above 12%) and at P22 on P/B among credit-services peers, a 50% discount to the sector median. That discount looks justified by ROE below peers, so the grade is fair, leaning cheap. The main worries are FY and next-FY EPS estimates cut about 5–6% over the last 90 days while 24 of 35 analysts still rate it buy, and no fresh Q2 asset-quality data. Stage 3 was 3.4% and Stage 2+3 8.2% at FY26, with ₹1,196 cr of impairment charges in H1.

SBI Card is India's #2 credit-card issuer, a mono-line lender with about 18.5% share of cards and 18.2% of spends, earning on revolver interest and fees. In Q2FY27 revenue was Rs 5,302 cr, up 3.2% YoY, and growth has slowed steadily from +10.1% in FY26 to +7.0%, +3.4% and now +3.2%. PAT jumped 74.8% YoY to Rs 778 cr (margin 14.7%, up from 10.5% in FY26), but that came from falling credit costs off a weak base, not from growth: receivables fell 2% YoY and card spends grew only 3%, while gross NPA improved from 2.41% to 1.90% and net NPA from 1.04% to 0.77%. On the lender yardstick (price-to-book against ROE, not P/E), 3.6x book against a 14.7% trailing ROE (18.4% in the latest quarter) is fair to slightly rich: it ranks P78 on P/B and P67 on trailing P/E among credit-services peers, though the stock sits near its 52-week low, the 16.3x forward P/E is below the 26x trailing, and FY EPS estimates were raised about 7% over 30 days. The main risk is that profit growth is coming from credit-cost relief while the loan book shrinks, and that lever runs out once asset quality normalises.

fundamental.thesis: HDFC AMC is one of India's top-two mutual fund managers, with about 13% QAAUM market share, roughly ₹9.3 lakh cr of QAAUM and around ₹6 lakh cr in equity AUM. It runs an asset-light, debt-free model whose earnings move with equity AUM and SIP flows; its retail franchise is strong, with 16.7M unique investors and SIP/STP flows of about ₹4,880 cr a month, up 33% YoY. The latest quarter we have read is Q1 FY27: revenue rose 13.6% YoY to ₹1,100 cr and PAT rose 12.0% to ₹837 cr. That is a slowdown from FY26, when revenue grew +17.8% to ₹4,122 cr and PAT grew +16.2% to ₹2,858 cr. The 'accelerating' revenue signal in the trend table reads the series in the wrong order, and two of its rows (Q4FY26 ₹41 cr, 9MFY26) have broken units, so we ignored them. One important caveat: the Q2 FY27 results filed on 2026-10-15 have not been read, so all figures here are one quarter stale. We graded valuation on earnings multiples suited to an AMC, as the sector card says, not on P/B against lenders. On that basis it is fair: 35.5x trailing and 27.4x forward P/E for a debt-free business with ROA around 29% and a payout near 80%. The 'expensive vs peers' tag and P/B of 11x compare it with banks and NBFCs, which is the wrong peer set, and the snapshot's 222% dividend yield and 2.36 debt/equity are data errors for a debt-free AMC. The stock sits at 26% of its 52-week range, which is a reasonable entry point. Against that, sell-side EPS estimates are being cut steadily (-1.4% over 30 days, -2.0% over 90 days) even though 25 of 27 analysts rate it Buy, which points to a slower earnings path ahead.

fundamental.thesis: Poonawalla Fincorp is a fast-scaling NBFC backed by the Poonawalla group, focused on consumer and MSME lending with an AUM of ₹74,008cr in Q2FY27 (up from ₹60,348cr in Q4FY26, a 22.6% HoH increase). The principal risk is that credit costs remain elevated at 2.19% and cost of borrowing continues to tick higher (7.76%, +4bps QoQ), delaying the RoA/ROE recovery the premium forward multiple demands and risking a sharp de-rating from an already near-52-week-low price.

fundamental.thesis: Sundaram Finance is a premium TVS Group NBFC with ~₹92,887cr consolidated group AUM spanning commercial-vehicle/vehicle financing, home finance (Sundaram Home Finance), asset management (Sundaram AMC), and general insurance (Royal Sundaram), known historically for conservative underwriting and best-in-class asset quality in the CV segment. Q1FY27 consolidated PAT surged +33.9% YoY to ₹636cr — a sharp re-acceleration from FY26's full-year +9.5% PAT growth — with ROA improving sequentially to 3.06% from 2.91%, net NPA declining to 1.35% from 1.71%, and loan growth holding steady at 17% YoY; the operating trajectory is genuinely improving even as AUM growth decelerates mildly (17% → 16% → 15% over three periods), and the group subsidiaries (home finance +37% PAT, AMC +13% PAT) add earnings diversification. Using P/B + ROE as the correct NBFC yardstick (per sector card — P/E explicitly deprioritised for lenders), P/B of 3.51× with estimated ROE ~15% (derived from ROA 3.06% × leverage multiple) rates as fair; trailing P/E of 23.35× is within the NBFC benchmark range (18–28×), but forward P/E ranks at P100 among Credit Services peers (+45.4% premium vs sector median 14.6×), signalling the stock is fully priced for near-term earnings, and the 52-week position at 42.8% of range offers only modest entry comfort in a RISK_OFF tape. The dominant structural risk is the Capital Adequacy Ratio declining from 20.0% to 18.5% over four consecutive periods, compressing balance-sheet expansion headroom and raising the prospect of a dilutive capital raise, while rising crude at $89.72 creates incremental stress on the CV borrower book precisely when macro conditions are already tightening.

Max Financial Services is a listed holding company whose value comes almost entirely from its 80.01% stake in Axis Max Life Insurance (Axis Bank holds 19.99%), one of the mid-sized private life insurers; life premium income was ₹10,187 cr of ₹11,601 cr consolidated revenue in Q2FY27. Q2FY27 revenue grew +18.5% YoY, in line with +18.2% in Q1FY27 and faster than +8.2% for 9MFY26 (though that period is not like-for-like). Consolidated PAT rose to ₹100 cr from a tiny ₹5.9 cr base, giving a PAT margin of about 0.9%, which says little about a life insurer whose value lies in embedded value and new-business margins. The right yardstick for life insurers is P/EV with VNB margin and APE growth, and none of those figures are in the data, so trailing P/E of 682.7×, P/B of 20.3×, ROE of 1.6% and EV/EBITDA of 69.1× all overstate how expensive it is. Even so, MFSL sits at P100 among listed life peers on forward P/E (102.3× vs median 46.0×), P/B and EV/EBITDA, and the holding-company layer usually earns a discount, not a premium. On balance I grade it fair with low confidence until P/EV data is available; the biggest risk is the pending MFSL–AMLI amalgamation, which needs IRDAI and shareholder approvals and could change the holding-company discount either way.

fundamental.thesis: Persistent Systems is a Pune-based mid-tier IT services company (~₹10,700 cr estimated FY26 revenue) specialising in digital engineering and cloud transformation for BFSI and Hi-Tech verticals, and one of the fastest-growing Indian IT mid-caps by revenue trajectory. Q1FY27 revenue grew +24.3% YoY to ₹2,866 cr (stable vs multi-quarter trend of +21–25%), and deal TCV has nearly doubled from $0.33B in Q4FY25 to $0.67B in Q3FY26 — a strong pipeline leading indicator that supports above-sector growth for at least 2–3 quarters ahead; PAT margin at ~16.9% (Q1FY27 per yfinance) shows modest compression vs prior year's 18%+ levels, suggesting cost build-up offsetting revenue scale. At trailing P/E 45.1× versus the IT sector median of 22–30×, and ranked P100 (most expensive in sector) across trailing P/E (+82.9% premium), forward P/E (+77%), P/B (+102%), and EV/EBITDA (+108%), the stock is unambiguously expensive with a significant premium that is only defensible if 23–25% revenue growth proves durable in a sector undergoing AI-driven deflation. Note: the multi-quarter trend table shows revenue in units inconsistent with yfinance quarterly figures (growth rates match but absolute levels diverge ~14×), reducing confidence in PDF-sourced absolute numbers; data_quality is therefore partial.

Coforge is a fast-growing mid-tier Indian IT services firm focused on banking, insurance and travel clients, and it continues to out-grow tier-1 peers. Q2 FY27 revenue was ₹6,171 cr (+53.6% YoY) with PAT of ₹588 cr (+56.5% YoY), quickening from +49.2% revenue growth in Q1 FY27; PAT margin held steady at about 9.5% and EBITDA margin rose slightly to 20.6%. The forward indicators also look strong: the 12-month executable order book is $2.38bn (+45% YoY), Q2 order intake was $1,040mn with 8 large deals signed, and guidance was raised. However, organic constant-currency growth was a much lower 5.2% QoQ in Q1, and the large AI-engineering and data service lines grew only +1.4% and -6.1% YoY, which suggests much of the headline growth is acquisition-led. On valuation, using P/E backed by EV/EBITDA and peer rank as the IT yardstick, trailing P/E of 32.95× is above the 22–30× sector range and at P88 vs peers. Forward P/E of 21.0× and EV/EBITDA of 15.8× (+7.6% vs the peer median, P67) are close to the peer median given roughly 50% growth, so the overall grade is fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that growth is mostly acquired rather than organic, with AI-driven deflation of legacy services underneath; a clear slowdown once the acquisition laps would hit the multiple.

Oracle Financial Services (OFSS) sells core-banking software (Flexcube and analytics) to banks worldwide; about 90% of revenue comes from products and roughly 73% from outside the USA, and it reported a high 44% operating margin in FY26. FY26 revenue was ₹7,672 cr, up 12.0%, with PAT of ₹2,639 cr, up 11.0%. The extracted H1 FY27 figures show revenue of ₹5,032 cr (+38.2%) and PAT of ₹2,118 cr (+78.2%, a 42.1% margin), a sharp step-up that we cannot yet confirm. The pre-computed 'accelerating' signal compares a half-year against annual periods, the quarterly rows are missing or have mixed units, and a +78% PAT jump in a licence business may include a lumpy one-off deal or other income, so we treat the acceleration as unverified. On valuation, using P/E and EV/EBITDA as the IT yardstick, a trailing P/E of 33.4x is above the 22–30x sector range and at the 82nd percentile of peers. EV/EBITDA of 23.7x is 56% above the peer median and the stock sits at 88% of its 52-week range, so it grades expensive even though the 26.3x forward P/E and 32.6% ROE point to expected growth. The main risk is that the H1 surge proves to be lumpy licence revenue or a data error rather than a durable step-up, which would leave a near-high, premium-multiple stock exposed to a de-rating in a risk-off tape.

Deepak Nitrite is India's largest producer of phenol, acetone, IPA and sodium nitrite. It is a specialty and commodity chemicals business, so it is judged on spreads, and roughly two-thirds of its revenue comes from the Phenolics segment, which earned a 13% EBIT margin in FY26. In Q1 FY27, revenue rose 36.4% YoY to ₹2,578 cr and PAT rose 207% to ₹345 cr, a 13.4% PAT margin. That is a sharp break from a weak FY26, when revenue fell 4.8% and PAT fell 20.5%, and Q3 FY26 grew only 3%. This is one strong quarter rather than a proven multi-quarter trend, and the 'accelerating' trajectory signal mixes annual and 9M periods, so it overstates consistency. Using EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive chemicals cyclical, the stock trades at 24.6× versus a peer median of 17.9× (P67) and the sector card's 5–8× mid-cycle norm, while trailing P/E is 41.6× against ROE of only 9.8%. Even allowing for the forward P/E of 27.6× and +17% 90-day EPS upgrades, that grades as expensive. The biggest risk is that the Q2 FY27 results filed on 29-Oct are not yet in our data, and rising crude (above $102) could squeeze phenol spreads just as heavy ₹2,500 cr FY27 capex is being deployed.

APL Apollo is India's dominant structural steel tube maker, with about 65% market share, a branded value-added mix and capacity of about 5 Mt targeted to reach 10 Mt by FY30, so it behaves more like a branded building-materials processor than a commodity steel mill. H1 FY27 revenue was ₹12,608 cr (+17.8% YoY) and PAT ₹646 cr (+19.8%), with EBITDA margin 8.5% vs 8.0% in Q1. Implied Q2 PAT of about ₹383 cr is roughly +27% YoY, or about +24% after stripping the ₹9.7 cr divestment gain, a clear step-up from Q1's +8.4% revenue and +10.9% PAT. However, implied Q2 revenue (₹7,001 cr from H1 less Q1) conflicts with the yfinance ₹5,899 cr, so the size of the quarterly revenue acceleration is unverified. Q2FY27 net sales grew +23.7% YoY to about ₹4,623 cr (trend table basis) and PAT grew +190.9% to ₹135 cr off a weak base, with real volume growth of 16% and premium volume growth of 38%. EBITDA margin expanded 480bps to 11.9% and PAT margin held at about 5.3%, so revenue growth has accelerated from +10.0% in Q1 to +23.7%. Gross margin is mixed, though: Q1FY27 was 41.0% against 44.1% for FY26, before a +194bps YoY gain in Q2. The Q3/Q4 FY26 rows are missing, so the multi-quarter trend rests on only 2 clean quarters. Forward P/E of 46x is inside the band but still at P83, so the grade is expensive, even though the stock sits near its 52-week low and P/B is at P17. The biggest risk is that the expected earnings recovery is not holding: next-FY EPS estimates have been cut 8.8% over 90 days, which threatens a stock priced for that recovery, while the ₹752 cr CCI penalty (about 2.3% of market cap, ₹188 cr already deposited) awaits a Supreme Court ruling.

Reported H1 FY27 numbers are weaker: revenue rose 107.8% YoY to ₹2,441 cr, but PAT fell 49.8% to ₹495 cr (12.6% margin). That PAT includes a ₹309 cr non-cash fair-value gain, so underlying profit is roughly ₹186 cr. Operating cash flow was negative at ₹-724 cr, and net debt rose from ₹7,607 cr in Q1 to ₹8,111 cr. The trend table mixes quarterly, half-year and full-year periods, so the 'accelerating' and 'contracting' labels are not reliable, and H1 FY27 bookings and collections are not in the data, which leaves a gap in the metrics that matter most here. I graded valuation on enterprise value to pre-sales (bookings) and P/B against ROE, not P/E, because reported profit here lags actual sales by 2–4 years. Enterprise value is about ₹59,500 cr, or roughly 1.7× FY26 bookings. P/B is 2.68× against ROE of 10%, and the stock sits at 25% of its 52-week range, so it looks fair, leaning slightly cheap. The biggest risk is that cash generation weakens while debt rises in a risk-off market.

fundamental.thesis: Aptus Value Housing Finance is a mid-sized affordable-housing lender in South India that makes small-ticket loans to self-employed and informal-income borrowers, and earns a high return on assets (ROA 7.76% in FY26). In Q1FY27 total income rose 17.0% YoY to Rs 428 cr and PAT was Rs 261 cr. The trend table shows PAT up +49.3%, but its Q1FY26 base of Rs 8 cr is clearly a bad extraction; the yfinance rows suggest about +19% PAT growth. Growth is slowing from +23-30% in FY26 to +17%, and AUM growth was only 12.2% in FY26, below Aptus's historical pace. Using P/B against ROE, the right yardstick for a lender, 2.69x book for a 20.1% ROE looks cheap. Trailing P/E of 14.5x (forward 10.5x) is also below the 18-28x NBFC range and sits at P13 vs the broad market. The main risk is asset quality: GNPA rose from 1.19% to 1.42% and NNPA from 0.90% to 1.07% while provision coverage is thin at about 25%, and the company keeps selling loans to ARCs at a loss. Q2FY27 results are due on 4 Nov and could confirm or ease this trend.

Bajaj Housing Finance is a large housing-finance NBFC in the Bajaj group, lending to home buyers, property owners and developers, with AUM up 25% YoY to ₹1,58,205 cr and asset quality that remains very clean (GNPA 0.29%, NNPA 0.12%). Q2FY27 revenue, derived as H1FY27 ₹6,314 cr minus Q1FY27 ₹3,063 cr, was about ₹3,251 cr, up about 18% YoY and faster than +14.3% a year earlier. PAT was about ₹757 cr, up about 17.7% YoY, and PAT margin has held flat near 23%. Under the surface, net interest income grew only 9.8% YoY against 24-25% loan growth, NIM slipped from 3.5% to 3.36%, credit cost rose to 0.52% in Q1FY27 from 0.15% in FY26, and capital adequacy fell from 26.1% to 21.2% as the book grew faster than equity. Using the lender yardstick the sector card asks for (price-to-book against return on equity, not P/E), a P/B of 3.19x for an ROE of only about 12-12.6% is expensive, even though it sits around the 36th-38th percentile against the broad market and the forward P/E of 19.9x implies expected earnings growth. The biggest risk is that loan growth keeps outrunning lending spreads and capital, while the CFO's resignation on 2026-10-23 adds governance and continuity uncertainty for a midcap lender running debt-to-equity near 4.9x.

fundamental.thesis: Bandhan Bank is a mid-sized private bank that grew out of microfinance; it now has 6,400+ outlets and 3.2 crore customers, but its book still leans towards unsecured, high-yield borrowers in East India. Profit is recovering mainly because bad-loan costs fell, not because the business is growing faster: credit cost dropped from 2.84% in FY26 to 0.44% in Q1 FY27, which lifted H1 FY27 PAT 132% YoY to Rs 1,123 cr, while income grew only about 4.9% YoY. Quality is improving at the same time, with NIM at 6.2% (from 6.1%), GNPA down to 3.1% from 3.3%, provision coverage up to 85.9% and Q2 advances up 13.1% YoY. Using the lender yardstick (P/B against sustainable ROE, not P/E), the stock looks fair rather than cheap: P/B of 1.35x is at P9 of the broad market, but trailing ROE is only 4.9% and Q1 ROA of about 1.0% implies high-single-digit ROE, so the low multiple mostly reflects low returns. With the price at about 95% of its 52-week range and a forward P/E of 9.9x that already assumes a full earnings recovery, the main risks are that deposits (+9.2%) are lagging advances (+13.1%) and that next-year EPS estimates have been cut 4.3% over 90 days.

fundamental.thesis: BSE is India's oldest stock exchange and a capital-markets infrastructure monopoly, earning revenues through transaction charges, listing fees, clearing/settlement, and investment income — it is not a traditional bank, so the relevant yardstick is P/E and EV/EBITDA (not P/B+ROE). Q1FY27 revenue grew +63.5% YoY to ₹1,566 cr and PAT grew +62.1% YoY to ₹873 cr at a 55.7% margin; while the absolute growth rate is still exceptional, the trajectory has decelerated from +116% in FY25, and PAT margins are broadly stable (55.7% vs 56.3% a year ago) rather than meaningfully expanding. At 48.1× trailing P/E (P68 vs broad peers) and EV/EBITDA of 28.4× (P63), the stock screens as fair against headline P/E metrics, but the forward P/E at 37.8× sits at P78 (expensive), P/B at 17.4× is at P94 (extremely elevated even for an asset-light exchange model), and sell-side EPS estimates have been cut sharply over the past 90 days (FY-EPS −6.6%, next-FY −9.8%) — a classic pre-derating signal that makes the 'fair' grade conditional on growth sustaining. The single biggest risk is that BSE's transaction-charge revenues are directly levered to equity market volumes and IPO activity, both of which face acute pressure from FII outflows of ₹44,000+ cr over 30 days, a RISK_OFF macro regime, and rising regulatory contribution costs (₹193 cr, +66% YoY), which could compress earnings faster than consensus currently models.

CAMS is India's largest mutual-fund registrar and transfer agent (RTA), an asset-light, fee-based capital-markets infrastructure business whose revenue tracks industry mutual-fund AUM and transaction volumes. Derived Q2 FY27 revenue was about ₹415 cr (+10% YoY vs ₹377 cr) and PAT about ₹130 cr (+13% YoY; the company's press release states +14.4% consolidated). Revenue growth has accelerated from +3.2% in Q2 FY26 to the +10-11% range over the last two quarters, though it eased slightly from Q1's +11.5%, and PAT margin has expanded from 29.6% to about 31%, backed by a 48% H1 EBITDA margin and 0.98x cash conversion. On an AUM-linked earnings yardstick rather than lender P/B, trailing P/E of 43.6x and forward P/E of 32.2x (EV/EBITDA 27.6x, P64 vs the broad market) look fair for a 39%-ROE, net-cash franchise, but the stock sits at 84% of its 52-week range and consensus EPS estimates have been trimmed about 1% over 30 days, so near-term upside looks limited. The main risk is that revenue is pure equity-market beta: in a risk-off tape with heavy FII selling, falling equity AUM or slowing SIP flows would compress fees, and the latest available AUM-growth KPI already slowed from 22% to 16%.

fundamental.thesis: Can Fin Homes is a mid-size Housing Finance Company (HFC) and Canara Bank subsidiary, focused on affordable housing (83% of portfolio) across 21 states through 250 branches — a niche lender with institutional parentage and a structurally low-cost origination model. PAT growth has re-accelerated from -4.3% YoY in Q1FY26 through +18% in Q2FY26 and +27% in FY26, sustaining at +20.2% in Q1FY27 (₹268 cr); H1FY27 PAT margin expanded to 24.4% from 22.4% in Q1FY26, and GNPA collapsed from 6.71% (Q1FY26) to 0.90% (H1FY27) while disbursement growth surged to 29% YoY in Q1FY27 — a leading signal for portfolio acceleration — though NIM has edged down from 3.93% (FY26) to 3.81% (Q1FY27), using the sector-card P/B+ROE yardstick for lenders, P/B of 1.74× against ROE of 17.15% grades clearly cheap (below the 1.5× threshold but with materially above-12% ROE), with the stock sitting at P5 in broad-market peers, near its 52-week low, and forward P/E of 8.23× below trailing 9.19× confirming further earnings growth priced in. The biggest risk to this thesis is NIM erosion accelerating: deposit repricing typically lags EBLR-linked asset yield cuts in an easing cycle, the LCR has already fallen from 250% in Q1FY27 to 100% at H1FY27 (the regulatory floor), and ISCR of 1.51 leaves a thin interest-coverage buffer if borrowing costs prove sticky.

fundamental.thesis: Canara HSBC Life Insurance (CANHLIFE) is a bancassurance-focused life insurer distributed primarily through the Canara Bank and PNB branch networks, giving it a structural reach advantage over standalone agency-model peers; however, for a life insurer the correct valuation yardstick is P/EV (Price-to-Embedded Value), not P/E, and P/EV data is absent from this pack. Revenue growth has been strong at +25% YoY in FY26 (peaking at +31.6% at 9M before settling), but PAT has grown only +8.5% as PAT margin contracted from 1.6% (H1 FY26) to 1.3% (FY26 full year), meaning topline momentum is not converting to bottom-line expansion — a concerning quality signal; crucially, H1 FY27 results were filed on 9-Oct-2026 but remain unextracted, leaving the current trajectory blind. As the best available proxy, P/B at 8.29× against a TTM ROE of only 8.1% is clearly expensive (P/B < 1.5 + ROE > 12% = cheap; this is the inverse), and broad-market peer rank at P94 on trailing P/E (107×, +205% vs median 35×) and P98 on forward P/E confirm top-decile expensiveness with no margin of safety. The single biggest risk is that thin, contracting PAT margins (1.3%) combined with a ₹287.5 cr NCD issuance signalling capital needs leave the earnings base fragile — any claims spike, cost overrun, or distribution slowdown would disproportionately impair an already leverage-heavy, low-ROE profile in a RISK_OFF macro regime where Financials are macro-underweight.

Capri Global Capital is a fast-growing diversified mid-cap NBFC with ₹43,878 cr AUM, now 48% in gold loans, alongside MSME, affordable housing and construction finance plus a fee-earning distribution arm. In Q2FY27, net total income rose 58.9% YoY to ₹1,085 cr and PAT rose 77.3% to a record ₹418 cr (38.5% PAT margin). Growth is keeping pace with recent quarters (AUM +62.3% YoY vs +62.0% last quarter), spread widened to 8.3% from 6.9% a year ago, cost-to-income fell to 41.4% from 49.4%, and RoAE climbed to 21.6% from 14.4%. On the lender yardstick from the sector card (price-to-book vs sustainable ROE), a P/B of 2.96x against 19-21% guided RoAE (16.5% trailing) is fair, not cheap, and the stock sits at 95% of its 52-week range; the 12.2x forward P/E and rising estimates (+7.7% over 30 days) support the growth story but leave little valuation cushion. The main risk is credit quality: provision cover on bad loans fell sharply from 43.2% to 33.3% QoQ while net Stage 3 rose from 0.6% to 0.8%, at a time of 3.8x debt-to-equity, a capital ratio down from 32.9% to 22.7% YoY, and heavy gold-loan concentration while gold prices are falling.

CreditAccess Grameen is India's largest pure-play microfinance lender, with a gross loan book of about ₹29,294 cr that grew 21.5% YoY as of H1 FY27 and 2,276 branches lending mostly to rural women borrowers. Asset quality is the real story: GNPA improved from 4.04% (9M FY26) to 3.17% (FY26) to 2.18% (Q1 FY27), with collection efficiency at 97.4% and provision coverage holding around 65%. The low forward P/E of 11x simply reflects the earnings normalisation, and analysts have raised FY EPS estimates by 9.8% in the last 30 days. The main risks are a fresh stress cycle in unsecured rural lending, a borrower count that is shrinking (-2.4% YoY) even as loan size grows, and a risk-off macro backdrop for a leveraged midcap lender.

Using the P/B+ROE lender yardstick mandated by the sector card, P/B 2.79× against ROE 13.9% places the stock in fair territory (not cheap: P/B > 1.5×; not expensive: P/B < 3× with ROE > 12%); peer-relative ranking at P27 in the broad market and a ~40% discount to sector median P/B, combined with forward P/E 14.7× vs trailing 22.5×, suggest the market has already priced in a meaningful earnings recovery. The primary risk is that loan/AUM growth deceleration (tracking toward low-double-digits) persists in a RISK_OFF macro environment with rising crude costs and an elevated credit cost base, stalling the earnings normalisation that currently drives the bull case.

Home First Finance is a mid-sized affordable housing lender. It lends to first-time, lower-to-middle-income home buyers, earns a high margin (NIM 7.0% in FY26) and a strong return on assets (ROA 3.95% in FY26). Working back from the H1 and Q1 filings, Q2 FY27 revenue was about ₹565 cr (around +19% YoY) and PAT about ₹170 cr (around +29% YoY), and H1 FY27 revenue was ₹1,105 cr (+18.8%) with PAT ₹330 cr (+31.6%). Profit growth is holding near 30% and PAT margin has edged up from 26.9% to about 30%, but growth is cooling: loan growth slowed from 31% (H1 FY26) to 23% (FY26), and revenue growth has settled near 19% from the low 30s a year ago. On the lender yardstick of price-to-book against ROE, a P/B of 2.74x for a 15.7% ROE is fair for a high-ROA affordable-housing franchise rather than cheap, though a forward P/E of 14.95x against a trailing 22.2x shows the market expects earnings to keep growing. The main things to watch are a thin 23.6% provision cover on a 1.74% gross NPA and a slowing loan book, at a time when risk-off markets tend to punish midcap lenders that rely heavily on borrowing.

IEX runs India's dominant power exchange, a capital-light platform business. It is tagged Financials, but the lender yardstick (P/B against ROE) does not fit, so I graded it on P/E and EV/EBITDA. The extracted filings report H1 FY27 revenue of ₹325 cr (+9.9% YoY) and PAT of ₹274 cr (+12.3% YoY), with revenue growth slowing from +19.3% in FY25 to roughly +10–11% now. However, the trend table does not reconcile with itself: FY26 revenue of ₹616 cr sits below FY25's ₹657 cr yet is shown as +14.6%, Q1 FY27 revenue of ₹158 cr sits below Q1 FY26's ₹184 cr yet is shown as +11.4%, a 111% EBITDA margin is impossible, and the jump in PAT margin from about 65% to 85% looks like a change in how revenue is defined rather than a real gain. So the growth and margin readings are low-confidence. On valuation, trailing P/E of 22.3x (forward 19.6x) is about 37% below the broad-market median and EV/EBITDA of 14.2x sits at P24, while the stock is near its 52-week low (9% of range); with a 39% ROE that looks fair to modestly cheap, but I grade it fair because the data is inconsistent and because a de-rating near the lows usually reflects a structural concern. The biggest risk is regulatory and policy change to how India's power-exchange market is structured, which could erode IEX's volume share and pricing power.

fundamental.thesis: IFCI is a government-owned Development Financial Institution effectively in run-off mode — its active lending business has collapsed, with the loan book shrinking -23.56% YoY to ₹1,194cr, and the company now derives income primarily from residual assets and investments rather than fresh origination. FY26 revenue grew a modest +2.5% to ₹2,069cr and PAT rose +5.7% to ₹181cr, with PAT margin recovering from -2.1% (H1FY25) to 8.7% (FY26), a directional positive — but this improvement reflects the tail of provisioning cycles on a dying book, not a genuine lending franchise revival; Gross NPA stands at a catastrophic 95.79% and CAR is deeply negative at -18.78%, far below RBI's regulatory minimum, meaning IFCI is technically insolvent on a banking capital-adequacy basis. Using P/B + ROE (the correct yardstick for a lender per the Sector Card — NOT P/E), P/B of 2.43× against an implied ROE of roughly 2% (₹181cr PAT ÷ ~₹9,100cr implied book) signals expensive — the P/B > 1.5 with ROE < 12% heuristic squarely flags this; trailing P/E of 119.29× (vs 12–18× bank sector median) confirms the same; forward P/E of 23.38× implies a heroic earnings recovery that is entirely dependent on the DFS-approved group consolidation/restructuring, a binary outcome with no earnings visibility. The single biggest risk is that the pending merger/amalgamation of IFCI subsidiaries fails to deliver value to minority shareholders, while the negative CRAR (-18.78%) and near-total NPA book leave no fundamental floor — any positive thesis is a restructuring bet, not a lending franchise bet.

The biggest fundamental risk is governance: the re-designation of co-founder R Venkataraman from Joint MD to Non-Executive Director on October 15 is a leadership change at a sensitive recovery juncture, compounded by a declining Provision Coverage Ratio (114% in Q3FY25 to 63% in H1FY26) and deeply negative cash conversion (CFO/PAT −7.34×), all of which limit conviction despite the appealing valuation.

Indian Overseas Bank is a Chennai-based public sector bank in a strong recovery phase: FY26 gross NPA fell to 1.42% from 1.83% at H1FY26, net NPA is 0.21%, provision coverage is 97.5%, capital adequacy is 19.78% and loan growth is 24.2% YoY. Q1FY27 total income was Rs 10,938 cr (+23.3% YoY) and PAT was Rs 1,716 cr (+45.7% YoY, 15.7% margin), faster than FY26's +15.4% revenue growth, though the pre-computed trend compares quarters, half-years and full years, so the acceleration is indicative only. The Q2FY27 and H1FY27 results filed on 26 Oct have not been extracted yet, and yfinance's unreliable Q2 PAT of Rs 1,963 cr only loosely suggests sequential improvement. On the bank yardstick of P/B plus ROE, P/B of 1.63x against ROE of 16.5% is fair, just above the cheap threshold of 1.5x; the trailing P/E of 11x, the anomalous 36.5x forward P/E and the broad-market peer rank are not meaningful for a lender. The main risks are a CFO change effective 1 Nov 2026 and NIM moderation for PSU banks in the easing cycle, since FY26 NIM of 3.35% is the latest available reading and loan growth above 24% may run ahead of deposits.

fundamental.thesis: IREDA is India's government-backed specialized NBFC for renewable energy financing, a structurally advantaged lender in the clean-energy transition with a loan book growing at ~21% annually; its PSU backing and sector tailwinds provide a durable franchise but are not substitutes for credit discipline. Valuation: using the P/B+ROE yardstick mandated by the sector card (the primary lens for lenders), P/B of 2.28× against ROE of ~13.6% falls in fair territory; however, the peer-rank data (P16 on trailing P/E, P13 on forward P/E vs broad market) and a trailing P/E of 16.1× sitting below the NBFC sector range of 18–28× are clear cheap signals — the stock near a 52-week low at 5.6% of its 52-week range reflects the market pricing in these asset-quality concerns, not oversight. fundamental.thesis: IRFC is the Government of India's dedicated financing arm for Indian Railways (82.9% government-owned after the June 2026 OFS). At 2.3x book for a 12.8–13.3% ROE and roughly 1.4% ROA, the stock is fair, maybe slightly full, for a low-margin, policy-driven financier. The 'cheap' peer reading (trailing P/E 18.7x, P20) compares IRFC with the whole market rather than with lenders, so I don't rely on it. The biggest risk is that further government stake sales add share supply while thin, shrinking spreads keep EPS growth near 10% even with strong loan growth.

SBFC Finance is a mid-sized NBFC that lends secured MSME loans and gold loans to small businesses. Its gross loan book stands at ₹11,161 cr and it is now classified as a Middle Layer NBFC. In H1 FY27, total income grew 29.9% YoY to ₹1,038 cr and PAT grew 28.1% YoY to ₹269 cr, a 25.9% PAT margin. Growth has been steady at roughly 28-31% for six reported periods: the 'decelerating' tag reflects only a slip from +30.7% to +29.9%, and PAT margin has moved in a tight 26-28% band. On the lender yardstick of P/B against ROE, a P/B of 2.71x for a 13.0% ROE is fair, not cheap. ROE is held down by low leverage despite a strong ROA of about 4.5%, the trailing P/E of 22.4x sits inside the 18-28x NBFC band, and the forward P/E of 18.4x plus modest upward estimate revisions (+2.3% to +2.7%) point to continued earnings growth. The main watch-item is that the fast loan book build is running ahead of provisioning: provision coverage fell to 42.2% from 46.2% and FY26 credit cost rose to 1.45%. That leaves less cushion if small-business credit quality turns in a risk-off macro.

fundamental.thesis: 3M India is the listed Indian subsidiary of 3M Company (US), operating across four segments — Safety & Industrial, Transportation & Electronics, Healthcare, and Consumer — a diversified industrial-technology business leveraged to India's manufacturing expansion and domestic consumption themes. Revenue re-accelerated to +19.0% YoY in Q1FY27 (₹1,423 cr, 5th consecutive double-digit quarter), but earnings quality is poor: the reported PAT of ₹233 cr and 16.4% margin include a ₹73 cr exceptional land-sale gain, core EBITDA actually fell 2.7% YoY despite 19% topline growth, PBT before exceptionals declined 4.3% YoY, and the Transportation & Electronics segment margin collapsed 703 bps to 13.5% due to INR/USD headwinds — a clear deterioration of underlying operating profitability. At a trailing P/E of 64.1× and EV/EBITDA of 36.5× — both materially above the Industrials sector median (28–45× P/E) and placing the stock at P80 on P/E and P77 on EV/EBITDA vs. broader market peers — the valuation grades expensive, with earnings recovery already embedded in the 42.2× forward P/E; the high Debt/Equity of 9.6× and 86% YoY surge in finance costs compound the balance-sheet risk. The primary risk is that INR depreciation and segment-margin compression persist into Q2FY27, and with no management guidance provided, any disappointment against elevated consensus expectations could trigger a sharp de-rating from peak multiples.

fundamental.thesis: Action Construction Equipment (ACE) is India's dominant crane manufacturer with a growing defence and construction equipment franchise, competing directly in the government-led infrastructure capex upcycle. Q1FY27 revenue surged +20.5% YoY to ₹786 cr — a sharp reversal from four consecutive quarters of YoY declines (trough: -11.2% in Q1FY26) — with PAT up +22.2% to ₹119.5 cr and PAT margin stable at 14.22%; critically, the crane segment drove +22.6% growth and a fresh Ministry of Defence order for backhoe loaders signals nascent defence revenue, while the balance sheet remains debt-free (D/E 0.00 in filings) with 33× interest coverage. At trailing P/E of 28× (at the lower bound of the 28–45× industrials sector range) and EV/EBITDA of 20.7× (below the broad-market peer median of 23.3× at P44), the stock screens as FAIR to modestly cheap — forward P/E at 21.5× below trailing confirms earnings growth is being priced in, and the EV/EBITDA yardstick (most appropriate for capital-goods names per the sector card) also supports a fair verdict. The biggest risk is that the growth recovery is a single-quarter data point after prolonged weakness, agriculture equipment remains soft (-6.4% YoY), there is no management guidance to anchor the trajectory, and industrials stocks historically de-rate 30–50% on any government capex-pause signal — a real risk given the current RISK_OFF macro regime with FII sustained selling.

Afcons is a midcap EPC contractor for marine, metro, tunnel and highway projects, so its revenue depends on executing and refilling its order book. That book is shrinking: order inflow fell from ₹15,960 cr in FY25 to ₹4,125 cr in FY26, the book slipped from ₹36,869 cr to ₹32,496 cr (2.7x revenue), and Q1FY27 revenue fell 20.2% YoY to ₹2,727 cr while PAT dropped 78% to ₹30 cr (1.1% margin). FY26 operating cash flow was negative (-0.51x CFO/PAT), and the new ₹3,469 cr Jewar expressway / Lucknow metro win is a real but partial refill. Using EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for capital-intensive EPC, 12.1x looks cheap against the broad market (P18), but that is not a tight infra-contractor peer set; trailing P/E of 46.9x is above the 28–45x Industrials band and P/B of 2.15x buys only a 4.7% ROE, so I grade it fair. The 19x forward P/E assumes a recovery while analysts have cut FY EPS estimates 18% over 90 days. Q2 results on 4 Nov are near-term event risk. Several data points look broken and the grade is held at fair rather than cheap because of them: Q1FY27 revenue is ₹2,727 cr in the trend table vs ₹1,878 cr on yfinance, Q1FY26 revenue shows an implausible ₹41,795 cr, the dividend yield reads 76%, and the consensus +49% upside conflicts with an implied price near ₹320.

fundamental.thesis: Apar Industries is a leading Indian maker of power conductors, transformer and specialty oils, and cables, and it benefits directly from the power-transmission capex cycle; its conductor order book reached a record ₹12,025 cr (+67.2% YoY), and Q2 new orders rose 123% to ₹4,775 cr. Q2 FY27 revenue grew 21.3% YoY to ₹6,931 cr, and H1 revenue grew 25.0% to ₹13,522 cr, in line with the steady +22-25% run-rate of the last four periods; H1 PAT jumped 77.7% to ₹915 cr as PAT margin widened from 4.8% to 6.8% and EBITDA margin from 9.2% to 11.8%. The growth is coming from price and mix rather than volume: conductor volumes fell 8.0% and oil volumes fell 16.9% in H1, and earnings did not convert to cash, with H1 operating cash flow at -₹863 cr (-0.94x PAT) after roughly ₹900 cr of inventory and ₹450 cr of receivables build, partly funded by a ₹2,500 cr QIP. On valuation (EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive name, cross-checked against P/E), it trades at 32.2x EV/EBITDA, 59.2x trailing P/E (above the 28-45x Industrials range) and 12.9x P/B, at P77-P90 versus the market, near 90% of its 52-week range, and about 3% above the mean sell-side target, so I grade it expensive despite strong delivery; the yfinance dividend yield (34%) and debt/equity (17.72) figures look like unit errors and are ignored. The biggest risk is a de-rating if margins built on high metal and base-oil prices normalise while volumes keep shrinking and US exports keep falling (-29.7% in Q2), which would expose the weak cash conversion at a premium multiple in a risk-off market.
